summary: Nabopolassar threw off Assyrian rule in 626 BCE and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria by 609 BCE. His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE) won Syria and the Levant at Carchemish, destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE and rebuilt Babylon in splendour. After his death three short reigns ended in Nabonidus, whose long absence in Arabia left Babylon exposed; Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BCE.
details: Babylonia had been ruled by Assyria for more than a century, and a civil war in Assyria after Ashurbanipal's death left the south unstable. Nabopolassar, a man of unclear origin who called himself 'son of a nobody', seized Babylon and Nippur in 626 BCE. The Assyrians struck back, retaking Nippur and besieging him at Uruk and in Babylon, but both sieges failed. On 22/23 November 626 BCE he was crowned king of Babylon. Babylonia was independent again, though it took nearly ten more years of fighting to push the Assyrians out completely.

By 616 BCE Nabopolassar was carrying the war into Assyria itself, but he could not break it alone. In 615 or 614 the Medes of western Iran under King Cyaxares invaded Assyria. In the summer of 614 BCE they besieged Assur, the ancient religious heart of Assyria, and sacked it brutally; even the hostile Babylonian chronicles were shocked. Nabopolassar arrived after the sack, met Cyaxares and signed an alliance against Assyria, sealed by the marriage of his son Nebuchadnezzar to Cyaxares's daughter Amytis. Together the two powers now had the strength to destroy the Assyrian Empire.

In 612 BCE the Babylonians and Medes joined forces against Nineveh, Assyria's capital and one of the largest cities in the world. After a siege of about three months, they broke through in August and plundered and burned the city, massacring many of its people. The Assyrian king Sin-shar-ishkun probably died defending it, and other Assyrian cities such as Nimrud were also attacked. The Assyrian heartland was lost; a remnant of the army fled west to Harran. Babylon now stood to inherit Assyria's lands in Mesopotamia, Syria and the Levant.

The last Assyrian ruler, Ashur-uballit II, held out at Harran in the west, backed by Egypt, which wanted Assyria to survive as a buffer against Babylon and the Medes. In late 610 or early 609 BCE the Babylonians and Medes took Harran. A few months later Ashur-uballit and an Egyptian army under Pharaoh Necho II tried to retake the city and failed, and Ashur-uballit disappears from history. Assyria was finished, but Egypt kept fighting, and Necho's army held Syria and the Levant as far as Carchemish on the Euphrates.

Necho II had made Carchemish, a key crossing and trading city on the Euphrates, his base in Syria. Around 605 BCE, Nabopolassar, perhaps ill, sent his eldest son and crown prince Nebuchadnezzar in sole command. Nebuchadnezzar crossed the river, crushed the Egyptian army and chased the survivors to the region of Hamath. News then came that Nabopolassar had died, and Nebuchadnezzar hurried back to Babylon, where he was proclaimed king in mid-August. The victory opened Syria and the Levant to Babylon and made it the dominant power of the Near East.

After Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar marched west almost every year to make the cities of the Levant accept his rule; the rulers of Phoenicia swore loyalty to him. In 604 BCE he attacked Ashkelon (Ascalon), a Philistine port on the coast, which had looked to Egypt for support. According to the Babylonian Chronicle its king was captured and taken to Babylon, and the city was plundered and levelled; excavations at the site confirm that it was largely destroyed then. The harsh example warned other cities in the region what rebellion would cost.

Even after its defeat at Carchemish, Egypt kept great influence in the Levant and encouraged cities there to resist Babylon. In 601 BCE Nebuchadnezzar took the risky step of marching across the Sinai to invade Egypt itself. According to the Babylonian Chronicle, both armies suffered huge numbers of casualties, and the invasion failed. Nebuchadnezzar spent the next year in Babylon rebuilding his chariot forces. Egypt was not conquered, and the setback may have encouraged Judah and others to rebel, though Necho II gave up his own ambitions in the Levant.

Jehoiakim, king of Judah, stopped obeying Babylon around 601 BCE, expecting help from Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar marched on Jerusalem in late 598 BCE, and the Babylonian Chronicle records that he took the city on 2 Addaru (March) 597 BCE and captured its king. Jehoiakim had died during the siege, and his young son Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) was taken to Babylon, where later records list him receiving food rations at the palace. Nebuchadnezzar installed Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah as king and carried off heavy tribute, keeping Judah as a vassal state.

Encouraged by Egypt, Zedekiah refused tribute to Babylon in 589 BCE. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, according to the Bible for 18 to 30 months, and in the summer of 587 BCE (some date it 586) took and destroyed the city and its temple. Zedekiah was captured, his sons were executed, and he was blinded and taken to Babylon. Much of the population was deported to Babylonia, beginning the Babylonian captivity, and archaeology confirms Jerusalem was destroyed and emptied. The Kingdom of Judah ended, and the southern Levant became a Babylonian province.

Tyre, a rich Phoenician port, had rebelled around the same time as Judah. Part of the city stood on an island about 800 metres off the coast and could not be taken without a navy. Nebuchadnezzar's siege is said to have lasted 13 years, usually dated c. 586 to 573 BCE, though the length comes only from the historian Josephus and is debated. The Babylonians destroyed the mainland town but never took the island. In the end the Tyrians negotiated a surrender, and Tyre remained under its own vassal kings, more tightly controlled by Babylon.

Nebuchadnezzar II ruled for 43 years, the longest of the Neo-Babylonian kings, and is remembered as the empire's greatest. Besides his wars, he rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale: the temple of Marduk (Esagila), the great ziggurat Etemenanki, palaces, the processional way and the Ishtar Gate. His later attacks on Egypt failed, and his empire's borders grew little after Carchemish. He died in Babylon in 562 BCE. His son Amel-Marduk followed, but was soon overthrown, the first of three short reigns that weakened the dynasty.

Neriglissar, who had seized the throne from Amel-Marduk, died in 556 BCE, and his son Labashi-Marduk became king. Within one to three months he was deposed and murdered in a plot probably led by Belshazzar, son of an elderly official named Nabonidus, who was then proclaimed king. Nabonidus was not of Babylonian royal descent; his mother came from Harran in former Assyria and was devoted to the moon god Sin. His favour for Sin over Babylon's great god Marduk soon set him at odds with Babylon's priests and leaders.

In 553 BCE Nabonidus left Babylon on campaign in Arabia and then stayed at the oasis of Tayma in northern Arabia from 552 to 543/542 BCE. Why he went is unknown, but quarrels with Babylon's priests and elite may be the reason. His son Belshazzar ruled Babylonia as regent, while Nabonidus remained king. Babylon's great New Year festival was suspended while he was away. When Nabonidus returned, he pushed his favour for Sin harder, rebuilding Sin's temple at Harran, deepening the anger of the Marduk priesthood as Persia grew stronger on Babylon's borders.

By 539 BCE Babylonia was the last great power in western Asia outside Persian control. In September or October of that year, Cyrus the Great invaded and defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris, north of Babylon. Sippar then surrendered, and on 12 October Persian forces entered Babylon. Babylonian sources say they took it without a battle, while Greek historians describe a siege. Nabonidus was captured but, according to several sources, spared, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, the last kingdom ruled by native Mesopotamian kings, passed to Persia.
